description: West African empire (c. 300–1235) controlling the gold-salt exchange at the southern Saharan frontier; Ghana's kings taxed all gold entering and leaving the empire, supporting a royal city of Kumbi Saleh described by Arab geographers as one of Africa's great trading centres; gradual Almoravid pressure and internal fragmentation weakened it before Sundiata's Mali empire absorbed its territories.

lifecycle_phases.description: Soninke Wagadou kingdom establishes control of Bambuk gold deposits; Arab and Berber traders begin regular trans-Saharan contact
Al-Bakri describes Ghana as one of the world's great kingdoms; Kumbi Saleh becomes major commercial city; gold and salt monopoly at maximum extent
Almoravid Berber confederation attacks from north; internal tensions between Muslim merchants and traditional rulers
Almoravid capture of Kumbi Saleh (1076); Ghana fragments; tributary kingdoms become independent; Sundiata's Mali absorbs remaining territories

rise_factors.description: Direct control of Bambuk and Bure gold deposits, the primary gold source for all medieval Saharan trade, gave Ghana structural commercial dominance
Position at the southern terminus of trans-Saharan routes allowed Ghana to tax all north-south commerce without possessing the Saharan routes themselves

decline_factors.description: Almoravid Berber military pressure from the north proved beyond Ghana's cavalry to counter in open desert terrain
